site.name: Caribou Ghost Town
overview: Caribou is a high-elevation ghost town northwest of Nederland that grew beside one of Boulder County's best-known nineteenth-century silver districts.

The settlement developed rapidly after rich silver discoveries on Caribou Hill in 1869, and surviving historical records document a substantial mining community shaped by repeated fires, epidemics, and the collapse of silver mining in the 1890s.

timeline.text: Prospectors identified rich silver-bearing veins on Caribou Hill, including the Caribou and Poorman lodes, triggering rapid development of the district.
A town had formed at Caribou; a federal mining history reported about 30 houses and 125 voters by November.
A major fire swept through Caribou, one of several disasters that damaged the settlement during its mining years.
The silver-price collapse and financial panic forced most mines in the district to close, accelerating Caribou's decline.
Another major fire struck the town, further reducing the surviving building stock.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey histories describe the Grand Island-Caribou area as a silver district west of Boulder and northwest of Nederland. By the end of 1871, most of the richest lodes had been located and production had expanded rapidly.

Late-1870s photographs preserved by the Carnegie Library for Local History show Caribou as a developed mountain settlement. The archive identifies the Sherman House in one view and notes additional views by William Henry Jackson.
Caribou Ghost Town is distinct from the nearby Caribou Mine, Caribou Ranch, and later recording-studio history. The townsite is represented separately as the historic settlement itself.
